h: A democracy of exclusion: when institutions bend, only the street is left
dek: NSUI's Anshul Trivedi argues that the Election Commission's failure does not stand alone. It is part of a long chain of institutions giving in, and the answer is satyagraha.
body: Anshul Trivedi is a national co-in-charge in the NSUI, the Congress party's student wing, and this piece is written from that side. He begins with the government's charge that the opposition leaders and ordinary citizens who took to Delhi's streets are anarchists. Trivedi agrees that the authority of institutions has weakened, but he says the blame lies not with the protesters but with those in power.

According to the writer, the Election Commission did not deny what came out about its internal workings. It only said the matters were being looked into. He alleges that this pushed many voters out of their right to vote, deepened doubts about several elections and broke trust in the voter rolls. In other words, this is not about one officer. It is a crisis of legitimacy.

Trivedi places this crisis in a bigger picture. He says the institutions that guard democracy bent before the executive one by one. He cites a Rajya Sabha election case and alleges that the state machinery was also used against critical media and individuals.

His complaint about the courts is just as clear. According to the article, more than 27 lakh (2.7 million) names were struck off the rolls in West Bengal during the SIR, and the Supreme Court said those left out would be able to vote in the next election. Later the appeals tribunal restored the names of 91 percent of the 82,782 people who appealed. The writer asks: if so many names were wrongly cut, how fair was the election?

Finally, Trivedi recalls the freedom struggle. Despite poverty and illiteracy, India gave every adult the right to vote, because for the oppressed this was the only road to equal citizenship. In his view, the Commission once worked to include as many people as possible, and now it is moving the other way. When institutions cannot stop it, satyagraha is all that is left, because this democracy came not from judicial review but from the people's struggle.
nazar: The 91 percent figure is a whole debate in itself. If nine out of ten people who appealed turned out to be right, what about the lakhs who had no time, papers or money to appeal? Exclusion hits hardest those who are weakest: migrant workers, poor women, minorities.

The writer belongs to a party, and his party's own record on institutions is not spotless either. Still, the question is bigger than his party. Universal adult franchise was this country's biggest promise, and if the fight to save it has reached the street, the fault lies not with the street but with the institutions.
sawal: Who will give back the vote to those who have no means to appeal?
ref: SIR
Special Intensive Revision, the Election Commission's drive to check voter rolls afresh. It is alleged that a large number of genuine voters lost their names in it.
Satyagraha
Gandhi's method of nonviolent resistance, in which people oppose injustice by peacefully accepting punishment instead of giving in.
ank: names cut in Bengal during the SIR

h: JP asks Modi: what is the difference between a declared and an undeclared Emergency?
dek: In Rajendra Sharma's satire, Jayaprakash Narayan holds up a mirror to the Prime Minister over a birthday greeting, and the lathis of Jantar Mantar keep coming into the conversation.
body: This satire by Rajendra Sharma, editor of the weekly Lok Lahar, begins with a coincidence of dates. According to the writer, Jantar Mantar was sealed off on 11 October and thousands of people, journalists among them, were beaten and detained. The very next day the Prime Minister wished Jayaprakash Narayan on his birthday and recalled the Emergency.

Sharma turns this greeting into an imagined conversation. JP, sitting in heaven, was not afraid of jail even when alive, and now fears nothing at all. As soon as Modi starts praising his fearless voice, JP cuts him short and asks why he uses the word Emergency so much when he himself never went to jail.

As the argument goes on, the Prime Minister offers the same arguments heard from the ruling side today: a conspiracy of anarchy, anti-national forces, an attempt to topple an elected government, and a developed India by 2047. JP replies that Indira Gandhi spoke exactly the same language, and her government was elected too. Opposing an elected government is a virtue of democracy, not a crime.

The sharpest part of the satire is a rapid round of questions and answers. Modi lists the excesses of the Emergency and JP puts a present-day example next to each one: arrests from homes, trains and airports, Delhi turned into a fortress, police brutality on the streets, censorship on the internet, courts putting off hearings, and gangs roaming under police protection. The writer's hint is clear: all this is being done to protect Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

In the end JP says he finds a declared Emergency better than an undeclared one, since at least it has a name. The Prime Minister loses patience and the meeting ends with a formal line about staying friends.
nazar: This satire makes you laugh less and stings more, and that is its strength. The memory of the Emergency has long been the government's old weapon to corner the opposition, but on the day after lathis fell at Jantar Mantar, that memory itself becomes a question.

There is a lesson in it for the movement too. If the government's language has begun to sound like the language of 1975, the answer must also come from that time: nonviolence, patience, and public support so large that undeclared curbs become meaningless.
sawal: What should a democracy call restrictions that are never declared?
ref: JP movement
A movement led by Jayaprakash Narayan in 1974 that began with students in Bihar and Gujarat. The Emergency was imposed in 1975 after it, and the Janata Party came to power in 1977.

h: Sir, why not give us Bharat Mandapam for protests?
dek: Lawyer Shahrukh Alam shows, with biting irony, that taking away Jantar Mantar and pushing protest to the city's edges really means pushing democracy to the margins.
body: This column by Shahrukh Alam, a lawyer practising in Delhi, is a polite petition on the surface and sharp satire underneath. A court had said that a designated protest site should be open, have facilities and not cause citizens trouble. The writer says that in that case Bharat Mandapam is the perfect place: in the middle of the city, inside a boundary wall. Why did the police not think of it?

The real issue is the standing order of 11 October that removed Jantar Mantar from the list of protest sites and named instead the Ramlila Maidan, for a fee, or Narela and Burari on the city's outer edge. In Alam's view this is a way to push protest to the edge of public life, both physically and mentally, just as the poor have been pushed out of Lutyens' Delhi.

She also counts the cost of this crackdown. Constables on duty for more than twelve hours, students and professionals losing whole days in detention, phones seized and never returned. She argues that Article 19(3) allows curbs on peaceful assembly only when public order is disturbed, a standard far higher than mere inconvenience. Yet the court took note of the metro closures, because they affected the general public, but put conditions on the protesters before hearing them.

The writer also records that some traders began cursing the protesters instead of the restrictions, and that charges like a threat of violence or a terror plot are stuck on every protest. Comparing with France, she points out that most sentences there were suspended and no place was banned permanently, while here, in four days after 17 October, fast-track trials of hundreds of people were wrapped up.

Her conclusion keeps the same irony: if the government truly cares about public inconvenience, let there be an independent public audit of the Chief Election Commissioner and the SIR, and let the Commissioner resign. The inconvenience will end on its own.
nazar: This piece reminds us that taking away the place to protest is also a way of crushing protest, only it uses fewer lathis and more paper. A protest sitting in Narela or Burari reaches nobody's ears, and perhaps that is the point.

On the day the Prime Minister was speaking at Bharat Mandapam, young people were being stopped from reaching the Election Commission. In a democracy, a stage for those in power and the margins for the people: this division is itself the biggest statement.
sawal: Who is a protest outside the city really meant to reach?
ref: Article 19(3)
The provision of the Constitution that allows reasonable restrictions on the right to peaceful assembly on grounds such as public order.
Jantar Mantar
The area near Delhi's 18th century observatory, which for decades has been the capital's main site for sit-ins and protests.

h: From 1942 to 2026: what if you are stopped before you gather?
dek: Jamia researcher Disha asks what the right to protest still means if people are detained before they can even put forward their demands.
body: Disha is a research scholar at the Dr. K. R. Narayanan Centre for Dalit and Minorities Studies at Jamia Millia Islamia. Her essay opens at Jantar Mantar on 10 October, a scene of barricades, heavy police and mass detentions. Protesters were demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the SIR.

She recalls that in June and July the Cockroach Janta Party demanded the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET paper leak, and he resigned on 25 July. This time the question is about the election process itself. In her view such allegations must be tested against evidence and scrutiny, but their legitimacy cannot be settled by stopping people from speaking.

She then turns to 1942. On 8 August the Quit India resolution was passed, and the very next day Gandhi and other leaders were arrested. She also mentions the 1930 Dharasana Satyagraha, where non-violent volunteers led by Abbas Tyabji and Sarojini Naidu were beaten with lathis (police batons). She says plainly that today's India is not colonial rule: it has a Constitution, Parliament and independent courts, so every restriction must be judged by constitutional standards.

That standard is Article 19, which gives the right to assemble peacefully and without arms, and also allows reasonable restrictions. From Supreme Court rulings such as the Ramlila Maidan and Shaheen Bagh cases, she concludes that neither indefinite occupation of public space nor unchecked bans on protest are acceptable. On 10 October, 45 Metro stations were shut. If smaller steps could have done the job, such sweeping restrictions are hard to defend.

She cites the Supreme Court's direction of 11 October that peaceful people must not be detained outside the law and that the Metro should run normally. Her conclusion: a democracy shows its strength by how well it can bear protest, not by how efficiently it silences it.
nazar: The strength of this essay is its restraint. A comparison with 1942 could easily have turned into sloganeering, but the writer honestly sets out both the differences and the continuity, and treats commuters' hardship as seriously as protesters' rights.

There is a useful lesson here for the movement: the language of courts and the Constitution is the street's strongest shield. A movement that passes the test of proportion and peace takes away the government's excuse to 'stop it in advance'.
sawal: Detention before demands are heard: is that a reasonable restriction?
ref: Article 19(1)(b)
This provision of the Constitution gives citizens the right to assemble peacefully and without arms. Under Article 19(3), reasonable restrictions can be placed on it for public order.
Dharasana Satyagraha
A non-violent raid on the Dharasana salt works in Gujarat in 1930, against the salt law. Reports of police beating unarmed volunteers with lathis drew attention around the world.

h: The lesson of Champaran: if the British gave way, why not this government?
dek: Aakar Patel recalls that in 1917 British rule made way for Gandhi's inquiry, while today's government is taking away the very right to gather in order to protect Gyanesh Kumar.
body: In this column, written two days after Gandhi Jayanti, Aakar Patel returns to the right to gather peacefully. He alleges that the government is stopping people from gathering in order to shield the Chief Election Commissioner from accountability, even though the facts about his work are now hidden from no one.

Then he tells the story of Champaran in 1917. Under the tinkathia system, farmers were legally bound to grow indigo on fifteen percent of their land. When the 47-year-old Gandhi arrived there, British officers first put him on trial, but soon understood that this battle could not be won. The case was withdrawn, Gandhi was allowed to hold an inquiry and thousands of farmers came to give statements.

According to the writer, the Lieutenant Governor made Gandhi himself a member of the inquiry committee. The committee ruled in the farmers' favour, recommended returning part of the money collected from them, and the nearly hundred-year-old tinkathia system came to an end. Patel says today's government should do the same: accept the right to gather and correct the injustice.

He recalls that this same government had to remove Dharmendra Pradhan over the failures in the exam system. Its hurried attempts to back off on the SIR, such as small changes in the process or a new form, are in the writer's eyes a sign of panic, and they have not cooled people's anger.

Patel argues that when a large part of the public takes to the streets, the government has to give way, as happened with the farm laws and the NRC. Gyanesh Kumar's term runs till January 2029, and the writer doubts the government can protect him that long, provided the movement stays united.
nazar: Patel's comparison is uncomfortable, and it should be. If a colonial government was ready to hear farmers' testimony, why should an elected government shy away from hearing the complaints of its own voters?

This piece was written before the movement fully spread, but its test still holds today: the question is not only about one officer, but about the crores of voters whose names are alleged to have been cut. The solution will be the one that gives them back their right.
sawal: Why is the government afraid of hearing its own voters' testimony?
ref: Tinkathia system
A system forced on Champaran by British indigo planters, under which a farmer had to grow indigo on three kattha of every bigha. It ended after the 1917 satyagraha.
SIR
The Special Intensive Revision of voter rolls. It is alleged that a large number of voters' names were cut in this process.

h: Cockroaches do not die so easily
dek: Writer R. Raj Rao draws on fables, Orwell and Chomsky to show why dismissing the Cockroach Janata Party as anarchists makes no sense.
body: This analysis by writer and professor R. Raj Rao was written at a time when several leaders of the Cockroach Janata Party were in detention. He fears that an anti-terror law like the UAPA could be used against the party's founder Abhijeet Dipke, and compares this with the case of Umar Khalid. Rao reminds readers that Dipke is a Dalit and an Ambedkarite.

Rao mentions the July Jantar Mantar movement, which he believes drew strength from Sonam Wangchuk's twenty-day fast. He asks whether someone will go on a long fast this time too, one that could press Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to resign.

Then he takes up a fable by the Marathi and English poet Arun Kolatkar. In it the government is the tiger, the Commissioner the shepherd, the people denied the vote the sheep, and Dipke the guard dog who may lose before the powerful. Echoing Orwell's Animal Farm, the writer alleges that today all voters are equal, but some are more equal than others.

The government calls the protesters anarchists. Rao answers with Chomsky's definition, in which anarchism means challenging authority that has no justification. In his view, the real stubbornness lies in keeping a system that gives one Commissioner unchecked power over votes and the cutting of names. He also notes that the police went easy on pro-government counter-protests.

Finally he targets the TV anchors who ask the party what its endgame is, or what its link with the Congress is. The writer says such questions are meant to divide the movement. And cockroaches, as the name says, do not die easily.
nazar: Rao's piece catches an important side of the movement: satire and symbols are its strength. A young generation dismissed as insects and vermin has turned that very name into its weapon.

But the movement still standing two weeks later shows that the question is not just about symbols, but about the right to vote. The more the government calls it a conspiracy, the more it will prove that it has few answers.
sawal: Will the ones called insects become the guardians of democracy?
ref: UAPA
The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, a harsh anti-terror law under which bail is very hard to get. Its use has often been questioned.
Arun Kolatkar
A well-known poet in Marathi and English (1932-2004), whose poem 'Jejuri' is seen as a milestone in Indian English poetry.

h: The days of women who suffer in silence are ending
dek: According to A.J. Philip's column in Qaumi Awaz, the most fearless faces at the front of the movement against the voter rolls belong to young women.
body: This column by senior journalist A.J. Philip appeared in Urdu in Qaumi Awaz, and it may be a translation of his original English piece. He starts with an old allegation recorded in Rajdeep Sardesai's book on the 2024 election, about women being frightened away from voting. The writer says any such trick would backfire today, because the woman who suffers quietly is now disappearing.

Philip lists a sequence. In the protests against the citizenship law, the women of Jamia, Aligarh and Shaheen Bagh were in front. Against the farm laws, they sat with farmers on Delhi's borders. Then, in the student movement demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, young girls were seen at the very front, and the government had at first taken them lightly.

Now the fight is over the Special Intensive Revision of voter rolls. According to the writer, during the tenure of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar more than thirteen crore (130 million) names were removed across 30 states and Union Territories, and later the Commission had to run a special drive to restore names wrongly cut. Philip sees this as a fight for a basic right of democracy.

Referring to viral videos, he writes that the girls refuse to obey police orders to move, ask under what authority they are given, and record every excess on their phones. They speak the language of the Constitution and know that a camera can turn any misconduct into a national issue within hours.

The writer also notes that many of the girls who have come to Delhi are from Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Rajasthan, and many of their parents stand with them. In his view this is not just a student movement but a big social change. In the end he says power may lie with the police, the government and the Commission, but the republic is not their property. It belongs to its citizens.
nazar: Philip captures the most underrated truth of this movement. The right to vote and the right to stand fearlessly on the street are two sides of the same coin, and this time both fights are being fought together.
We should also ask how many of the removed names belong to women. If being dropped from the rolls has hit them hardest, it is no accident that they are at the front.
sawal: How long can women who are no longer afraid be kept off the rolls?
ref: Shaheen Bagh
An area of Delhi where women held a sit-in for months in 2019-20 against the Citizenship Amendment Act. The sit-in ended after the Covid pandemic.

h: Ten years of Najeeb: the idea of JNU on trial
dek: Pallikonda Manikanta asks why JNU, known as a stronghold of dissent, could not bear a question raised about itself.
body: On 15 October 2016, JNU student Najeeb Ahmed went missing from the campus. A day earlier there were reports of a clash between him and ABVP activists. Ten years later, no one knows where he is. In June 2025 a Delhi court accepted the CBI's closure report, and in December that year the High Court upheld the decision.

The writer has been part of JNU politics since 2015. He accepts that the campus came to be known as a place of equality, plurality and dissent, but argues that an institution's character is decided not by its stated values but by how it behaves in a hard moment. The movement for Najeeb was that moment, when the question was asked not of outside forces but of the university itself.

According to the writer, when students surrounded the administrative building, the debate shifted from Najeeb's disappearance to the inconvenience of officials. On Karva Chauth, the wives of the Vice Chancellor and the Registrar came to the building, this was spread on Twitter, and pressure built to end the gherao (blockade). He does not question these women's feelings, but reminds us that Najeeb's mother Fatima Nafees, searching for her son, never got such sympathy.

The larger argument of the piece is that the call for progressive unity often covers up inequality within. In the name of a shared goal, people on the margins are told to set aside their particular complaints. The writer says this is not a failing of JNU or the Left alone. Every movement must look at whose voice is heard and whose pain is counted.

In the end he says pride in the past is meaningful only when we ask who was included in that past, and on what terms. This piece first appeared in English in The News Minute, and its Hindi translation has been published in Forward Press.
nazar: Najeeb's case is not only about one student. It is a test of how seriously our institutions take the disappearance of a Muslim student. The courts have closed the file, but a mother's wait has not ended. A campus that takes pride in fighting repression from outside must also account for the silences within.
sawal: Since when has asking where Najeeb is become a crime?
ref: Najeeb Ahmed
A biotechnology student at JNU who went missing from Mahi-Mandavi hostel in October 2016. Investigations by Delhi Police and then the CBI could not trace him.
Closure report
A report in which an investigating agency tells the court that it found no evidence fit to take the case forward. The court can accept it and close the case.

h: Brazil votes today, but the right has already won
dek: Bruno Cava argues that whoever becomes president, the Bolsonaro camp has shifted the balance of power through Congress, public money and pressure on the Supreme Court.
body: Brazil holds the second round of its presidential election on 25 October. The contest is between Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a prison sentence. According to Bruno Cava, an essayist and researcher in international relations at the University of Brasilia, whatever the result, the right has already tilted the country's politics in its favour.

In the first round Flavio got about 47 percent of the vote and Lula 45 percent, and later surveys show the gap has almost vanished. Flavio's agenda is a hardline one: declaring gangs narco-terrorists, five lakh (500,000) new prison places, making it easier to own guns and lowering the age of criminal responsibility. Cava reminds readers that Lula too has spoken in favour of lowering the age to 16 for serious crimes, meaning that toughness is no longer the language of the right alone.

The real change has come in Congress. In the 513-seat lower house, Bolsonaro's Liberal Party rose from 97 to 121 seats, while the Left stayed roughly where it was. The writer says this gain came mostly at the cost of other right-wing parties, and that a large majority of the new members are old politicians who switched parties.

The second front is the Supreme Court. The number of senators who talk of removing Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw Jair Bolsonaro's trial, has reached close to two-thirds. The third front is money: the budget for local projects in the hands of members of Congress has grown more than four times in 11 years.
Cava concludes that even if Lula wins, he will have to bargain with a stronger and more hostile Congress for every welfare scheme.
nazar: This piece shows that in a democracy, power does not live only in the presidential palace. Congress's budget, pressure on the courts and the politics of fear of crime can together tie the hands of any elected government.

The lesson for India is clear too. When every party starts speaking the language of jails, guns and punishment, young people from poor neighbourhoods are the first to be caught in it, whatever the colour of the government.
sawal: Can a government lose even after winning the election?
ref: Flavio Bolsonaro
A Brazilian senator and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. Since his father went to prison, he has been the face of the right-wing camp.
Alexandre de Moraes
A judge of Brazil's Supreme Court who oversaw the case of the plot to overturn the 2022 result. Bolsonaro supporters see him as a symbol of political revenge.
photo_note: Brazil's Congress in Brasilia, representative image

h: Why is Muslim politics always kept under suspicion?
dek: Responding to criticism of Sharjeel Imam's interview, Shaheen Kattiparambil asks why only autonomous Muslim politics is asked to explain itself.
body: In September 2026 Sharjeel Imam gave an interview to The Quint in which he spoke of an autonomous politics for Muslims and of decentralising power. Amana Begam, K.B.S. Sidhu and Ibn Khaldun Bharati wrote critiques of it from different angles. Shaheen Kattiparambil, who teaches at the University of Leeds, says all three share one basic assumption: Muslims organising on their own strength is treated as suspect from the start.

The writer compares how Dalits did identity politics through the BSP, the South through Dravidian politics, and Hindu nationalism through its own organisations. All were opposed, but only Muslim demands are instantly read as communalism, separatism or a threat to national unity. In his view, majority symbols are taken as national, while a claim to Muslim identity is called communal.

Sidhu points to constitutional guarantees and to Muslims who have reached high office. The writer says this is participation on paper; the real question is political power, and calling minority rights the generosity of the Constitution makes Muslims objects of pity, not equal citizens. He finds Begam's worry about elite domination valid, but says rights do not last without representation.

The writer accuses Bharati of calling Sharjeel's programme a Pakistan inside the country and of building a permanent Muslim motive out of centuries-old Muslim rule. He also says that calling Dalits and Adivasis (indigenous communities) someone's foot soldiers denies their own political understanding, and recalls Ambedkar's disagreement with the caste Hindu order.

The final point of the piece is Sharjeel's detention. He has been in jail since January 2020 and his trial is not over. According to the writer, the whole debate rests on his ideas, while there is little talk of such a long imprisonment. He concludes that Muslims are accepted as victims, as a protected minority and as citizens, but not as free actors who decide their own politics.
nazar: Whether or not one agrees with Sharjeel's ideas, in a democracy ideas are debated, not jailed. Six years of imprisonment without a verdict is itself proof that a Muslim voice is first heard as a threat. A republic that trusts its Constitution should give him a trial or set him free.
sawal: Why should only the politics of equal citizens be asked to explain itself?
ref: Sharjeel Imam
A JNU researcher who studied at IIT Bombay, facing sedition and UAPA cases over speeches made during the 2019-20 protests against the citizenship law. He has been in custody since January 2020.
Cabinet Mission Plan
A 1946 British government plan that proposed a loose union with a weak centre and groups of provinces, so that power could be handed over without partition.

h: From Paris to Delhi, inequality is at the root of young anger
dek: Oscar Berglund says the Gen Z movements in France, Spain and India are not separate complaints but the product of one structural crisis.
body: Oscar Berglund, who teaches international public and social policy at the University of Bristol, ties today's youth revolts together with one thread. In France, five to eight lakh (500,000 to 800,000) people took to the streets last weekend against run-down schools. In Spain, the death of an 87-year-old woman after an eviction sparked anger, parliament rejected a law to stop evictions, and now early elections are due there.

India gets a special mention in the piece. According to the writer, the Cockroach movement has emerged as the biggest challenge for the Modi government. At its root is anger over more than thirteen crore (130 million) names being cut from voter rolls, and its leader was arrested last week.

In Berglund's view this inequality is of two kinds. One is of class: since the 2008 recession, the gap in income and wealth has grown in Europe, and austerity has hollowed out schools, hospitals and care. The rich buy better services, the rest are left behind. The other is of generation: young people today are worse off than their parents and grandparents.

The standard of education is falling, AI is swallowing entry-level jobs, a large part of earnings goes on rent, and the climate crisis is making the lives of children born in 2020 far less secure. Efforts to rein in social media and AI are slow because of the tech companies' lobby.

Governments have mostly responded with repression: anti-protest laws, arrests and police force. The writer believes that in France and India this has fanned the fire further, and that without real steps on inequality, a political crisis is certain.
nazar: The young people on Delhi's streets are often called misguided or said to be acting on someone's signal. This piece reminds us that Paris and Madrid face the same questions: education, housing, jobs and the right to be heard.
When a generation feels its future will be worse than its elders', the lathi cannot silence it. Governments must talk about schools, hospitals and the voter rolls instead of arrests.
sawal: Why should a generation robbed of its future stay silent?
ref: Gen Z
Roughly the generation born between 1997 and 2012. Its movements have shaken governments from Nepal, Kenya and Bangladesh to Europe.
Austerity
Cutting spending on public services in the name of reducing the government deficit. It became common policy in Europe after the 2008 recession.

h: Soil is alive, stop treating it as a chemical store
dek: Sunita Narain argues that farm health depends on the tiny organisms in soil, not on sacks of fertiliser.
body: Sunita Narain, who heads the Centre for Science and Environment, calls soil the next gold in her latest piece. She argues that the ground beneath our feet holds the key to two things: raising farm yields, and locking away the carbon that is pushing the planet's temperature towards dangerous levels.

She compares soil to the human gut. Our health rests on trillions of microbes living in the gut, and how varied they are depends on what we eat. Sugary food feeds a few opportunistic bacteria, while varied, natural food sustains a rich living community. In the same way, she says, soil is a living system whose health is decided by bacteria, fungi, algae, earthworms and beetles, and their variety is tied to the variety of crops grown.

Her criticism is that the government and farm science still treat soil as a chemical account. The Soil Health Card measures nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, organic carbon and minerals such as zinc, magnesium and copper, but not the living part of the soil. The subsidy on chemical fertiliser stands at Rs 1.71 lakh crore, about three per cent of the annual budget, and India is the world's largest importer of these chemicals. She estimates that with supplies disrupted by war in the Gulf, the subsidy could double this financial year.

Down To Earth analysed 1.3 crore (13 million) soil health cards from 2023 to 2025. She writes that even though chemical fertiliser use rose by 20 per cent, soils remain badly short of nitrogen and other nutrients, and nearly half the samples were low in organic carbon. The result is that farmers' costs are rising while their earnings fall.

Her conclusion is that life needs life. A new science is needed to measure and understand the biological health of soil, because time to cut emissions is running out fast, and the work of returning carbon to the ground lies with these tiny creatures.
nazar: This is not just a scientific debate. It is a direct question of the farmer's pocket and the public purse. Every year there are more sacks of fertiliser, a bigger subsidy bill and greater dependence on imports, yet the fields stay hungry. Such a policy keeps companies and the import trade running, not the soil or the farmer. If the government put even part of this money into organic farming, crop diversity and monitoring soil life, farming would become cheaper and better for the climate too.
sawal: Why are our fields still hungry despite billions spent on fertiliser?
ref: Soil Health Card
A central government scheme started in 2015 that tests farm soil and gives farmers advice on nutrients and fertiliser. It does not measure the biological health of soil.
Soil carbon
Organic carbon stored in soil, which raises fertility and keeps carbon dioxide from the air locked in the ground. Microbes play a key role in holding it there.

h: Pakistan's stability: the books look better, ordinary people do not
dek: A Dawn editorial says that if economic stability won by squeezing demand is not turned into productivity, Pakistan will slide back into the same crisis.
body: In its editorial, Pakistan's newspaper Dawn uses the World Bank's latest report to point to an old cycle. The report estimates that if Pakistan's policies and institutions matched those of an average middle-income country, annual growth could reach six to seven percent, and by 2050 incomes could triple to reach Vietnam's current level.

Reality is far from this. Real growth in the last financial year was 3.65 percent and the primary surplus was 2.9 percent of GDP, but per capita income is rising by only 1.6 percent. In other words, the government's accounts have improved, people's lives have not.

According to the editorial, this stability came by crushing demand: high interest rates, tight budgets and costly electricity cooled the economy and cut imports. Money sent home by people working abroad and fresh loans filled the reserves, but these do not raise domestic production, and loans only push repayment further down the road.

The trouble is that as soon as growth picks up, imports of machines, fuel and raw material rise, exports do not keep pace, reserves fall and the government hits the brakes again. The paper says Pakistan has repeated this story many times.

As a cure, the editorial calls for bringing under-taxed sectors into the tax net, lowering the total cost of the power system, taking exports beyond mere concessions, and long-term investment in education, health and trustworthy institutions.
nazar: This debate is not only about Pakistan. In India too, GDP figures and the shine of the stock market often hide the truth seen in per capita income, jobs and prices.
Stability that comes by shrinking the ordinary person's plate may count as success in an economics textbook, but not in a household budget.
sawal: If people are not part of the growth, whose growth is it?
ref: Primary surplus
The gap between government income and spending, leaving out interest payments on debt. A surplus means that, interest aside, income is more than spending.

h: Neha Bora refuses: we will not sign the peace bond
dek: A day after the Delhi High Court gave no relief, the AISA president said that in its present form the bond goes against the democratic right to dissent.
body: Neha Bora, national president of the All India Students' Association (AISA), held a press conference on 24 October at the parliamentary office of the CPI(ML) Liberation in New Delhi and announced that neither she nor her organisation would sign the Delhi Police's peace bond. A day earlier the Delhi High Court had refused to give relief on her plea against the notice.

The matter goes back to 16 October, when police detained Bora during a Tiranga (tricolour) march held to demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and to protest irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls. The next day a notice came asking her to furnish a bond of ten thousand rupees and one surety until an inquiry before a special executive magistrate was over, so that peace would be kept.

Bora said this condition clashes with the right to dissent, and the courts must look at how such bonds are being used. She said future protests demanding the Election Commissioner's resignation cannot be called a breach of peace. She also asked: if citizens cannot question the government, whose peace is this?

Bora alleged that 50-60 right-wing people surrounded the Mandir Marg police station and raised slogans, and the police did not remove them, while slogans by the Election Commissioner's opponents were called a threat to peace. The report records no response from the police.
nazar: The peace bond was a tool made to prevent crime, but when it is used on students asking questions on the street, it becomes a way to put a price on protest. A student leader's refusal to sign opens a new front in this movement, and puts a question before the courts: how far is it fair to tie down dissent in advance?
sawal: Since when did raising slogans become a breach of peace?
ref: Peace bond
Under the law, an executive magistrate can make a person sign a bond to keep the peace. If the condition is broken, the money can be forfeited and there can be jail too.
SIR
The Special Intensive Revision of voter rolls, in which voters must show papers again to get their names entered. It has faced allegations of names being cut on a large scale.

h: Taslima's claim is wrong: Left bookstalls go up at Eid and Christmas too
dek: An Alt News check shows that Left groups' bookstalls in Bengal do not go up only at Durga Puja, and they do not sell only books on atheism.
body: Bangladeshi writer Taslima Nasreen wrote on Facebook on 20 October that in West Bengal the Left sets up bookstalls at Durga Puja but not at Christmas or Eid, and asked why atheism is promoted only during a Hindu festival. The post got more than seven thousand likes and more than 1,300 shares, while comments were turned off.

According to Alt News, both claims are wrong. The SFI and DYFI have set up stalls at Christmas near Kolkata's Park Street for at least ten years, which a newspaper even reported in 2016, and photos from 2017, 2022 and 2024 exist. This year at Eid, a local committee in Khidirpur set up a stall for two days.

The range of books does not match the claim either. The stall at the Jadavpur 8B bus stand had Bangla classics, poetry, history and books on Ramakrishna and Vivekananda. The stall near the Kalighat temple had works by Tagore, Bankim Chandra, Sarat Chandra and Bibhutibhushan, and one buyer's bag even held a book on Lalon Fakir.
The post came at a time when Left bookstalls had been torn down in Jadavpur on 17 October. Taslima, who left Kolkata in 2007, returned in July 2026, after a BJP government was formed in the state.
nazar: In Bengal a bookshop is now a political target, and a famous name's false claim gives that targeting a moral cover. Bulldozers on bookstalls and the 'anti-Hindu' label on social media seem to be parts of the same story. A society that begins to fear books should examine its fear.
sawal: Who feels threatened by a bookstall?
ref: Alt News
An Indian fact-checking website started in 2017 that investigates false information spread on social media.
photo_note: Representative image: a street in Kolkata

h: West Midnapore: Christian families attacked, pressed to give up their faith
dek: Three families in Patlapur village allege that during Durga Puja, men claiming to be from the Bajrang Dal beat them, threatened them and forced them to perform a puja.
body: Three families in Patlapur village of West Bengal's West Midnapore district allege that between 18 and 20 October they were attacked by a group claiming links with the Bajrang Dal. These families adopted Christianity some years ago and say relatives have been threatening them over it since last year, and no action was taken on an earlier complaint.

According to the FIR, the families were threatened with rape and death if they did not give up their faith. The complainant, Laxmi Mandal, was made to take a public 'purification' bath, and on 19 October she was taken to a puja pandal. It is alleged that she was hit on the head and her clothes were torn, and that two teenage girls of the family were also threatened, one of them choked by the throat. It is also alleged that on 20 October two men were taken from their home and threatened, and about twenty thousand rupees were stolen.

A case has been registered at Chandrakona police station against 13 named and some unknown people under sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, including attempt to murder and assault with intent to outrage a woman's modesty. According to SP Papiya Sultana, the complainant's statement will be recorded before a magistrate. No arrest had been made by 23 October, and the families have been given police protection.
Alt News has recorded 35 incidents against small Christian communities in Bengal between 1 July and 20 September. A Christian organisation is preparing to send a fact-finding team.
nazar: The Constitution gives the right to change one's faith, but in the village its price is being collected through beatings and 'purification'. Thirty-five incidents in three months are not a coincidence but a pattern. Registering an FIR is the first step; the real test is whether the police reach the people named.
sawal: Who is deciding the punishment for changing one's religion?
ref: Section 164 statement
A statement recorded before a magistrate, which carries more weight in court because it is taken without the police present.

h: Keralam government again takes Vigilance 'T' branch out of RTI
dek: A notification dated 22 October reverses a decision that was withdrawn in 2022 after a challenge in the High Court.
body: The Keralam government has taken two sections of the 'T', or Top Secret, branch of the Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau out of the reach of the Right to Information Act. According to a gazette notification issued on Thursday, 22 October, these sections handle sensitive material such as intelligence reports and confidential reports on government officials.

The government has used Section 24(4) of the RTI Act, 2005, which allows state governments to exempt intelligence and security organisations from the law. But the same section clearly says that information about allegations of corruption and human rights violations is not covered by such an exemption. According to the report, preparations for this step began last year, under the previous Left Front government.

This is not the first time. In 2016 too, the state had removed the T branch from RTI. The Indian Association of Lawyers and the Aam Aadmi Party challenged that in the Kerala High Court, after which the notification was cancelled in 2022. The new notification overturns that decision.

Several departments in the state are already exempt, such as the Special Branch CID, Crime Branch CID, the Crime Record Bureau, the Police Telecommunication Unit, forensic science laboratories, the Finger Print Bureau and the Home Department's special sections A and B in the Secretariat. The report recalls that neighbouring Tamil Nadu recently withdrew a similar exemption for its law and order department after political and public pressure. The report gives no reason from the government for this decision.
nazar: When the very agency meant to catch corruption starts avoiding transparency, questions are bound to follow. Quietly bringing back, through the gazette, a decision that could not survive in court, and without giving any reason, does not sit right with citizens' trust. The condition in Section 24(4) exists on paper, but when an entire office is shut, who will decide which file concerns an allegation of corruption? The government should at least make its case in public.
sawal: Why should an anti-corruption agency avoid transparency?
ref: Section 24(4)
The RTI Act provision that lets a state government exempt intelligence and security organisations. Information on allegations of corruption and human rights violations must still be given.
Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau
Keralam's agency that investigates corruption cases against government employees and officials.

h: In Kichha, 5,359 objections by one worker accepted, Muslims targeted
dek: According to a Newslaundry investigation, bulk objections by a BJP-linked booth agent in Uttarakhand's Kichha were first returned, then accepted after a complaint to the Commission.
body: In the Kichha Assembly seat of Udham Singh Nagar district, the final voter roll published on 3 October was missing 4,390 names that were present in the draft roll. According to the report, 6,884 Form 7 objections were accepted here, and 5,359 of them were from one man, Rajesh Tiwari, a BJP-linked booth agent and coordinator of a district cell. Most of the objections were against Muslim voters.

Tiwari himself said the Electoral Registration Officer had first returned the bulk objections, saying the rules had no provision for them. He then complained to the Election Commission by email, and within two days the office called him to submit the objections. The officer, Gaurav Pandey, neither confirmed nor denied this, and only said everything was done by the rules.

Timing is also in question. The deadline for claims and objections ended on 13 August, but approval of 504 of Tiwari's objections is dated 14 August. Of the 4,390 missing names, 3,720 had no objection against them at all; they were removed on the ground of 'logical discrepancy'.
Kichha's Congress MLA Tilak Raj Behad alleged that the objections were based on false information. The Commission did not answer the reporters' questions.
nazar: More than five thousand objections from one man, accepted under pressure from above after the officer had said no: this is an alarm bell for any electoral system. The Commission later put a limit on Form 7, but there is still no clear way back for those whose names have already been cut.
sawal: How can one booth agent get so many votes cut?
ref: Electoral Registration Officer (ERO)
The officer in charge of an Assembly constituency's voter roll, who decides on applications to add and remove names.

h: Papers given, name still cut: the voters of Kichha tell their story
dek: Muslim voters in Sirauli Kalan and nearby areas say their names were removed even after they answered the notices, and now they are being told to apply as new voters.
body: The second part of Newslaundry's investigation is about the voters of Kichha whose names were removed from the final roll after objections by BJP-linked booth agent Rajesh Tiwari, or without any objection at all. Most of them do not even know Tiwari. Many objections gave the reason as 'already enrolled', but the notices the voters received gave other reasons, such as an age mismatch or parents' details not matching.

Kulsum, 25, of Sirauli Kalan submitted her Aadhaar, family register, ration card and details from the 2002-03 roll. The officer assured her, yet her name was cut. Farman, 26, says he was born in Kichha itself and voted in 2022 and 2024; he got no notice and no call from the BLO (booth level officer). Five of the six names in the family of Ismail, 72, were removed, four of them his children.

Many families are now being told to fill Form 6, which is meant for first-time voters. Petitioners in the Supreme Court have already said that this counts old voters as new ones, and also puts them at risk of punishment for a false declaration.
The officer, Gaurav Pandey, said whatever happened was done by the rules. The state's Chief Electoral Officer and the Commission did not answer the questions sent to them.
nazar: Names being cut even after papers were submitted again and again shows that this process puts the burden of proof on the voter and shields the officer from any accountability. Asking people who have voted for decades to become new voters is a silent question mark on their citizenship.
sawal: Why should a voter of many years have to become a new voter?
ref: Form 6
The application to enter one's name in the voter roll for the first time, which requires a declaration that the applicant is not enrolled anywhere else.

h: Siang dam: protest and repression go hand in hand in Arunachal's villages
dek: Villages of the Adi community are on the streets against a study for the 11,000 megawatt project, and the response is forces, notices, a CBI case and curbs on news.
body: Village protests have grown against the proposed 11,000 megawatt Siang Upper Multipurpose Project in Arunachal Pradesh's Siang and Upper Siang districts. Three sites have been considered for the dam, including the villages of Uggeng and Komkar. On 14 September the government deployed hundreds of police and paramilitary personnel in these villages so that a pre-feasibility study could be carried out, and the villagers blocked the roads.

On 30 September, during Chief Minister Pema Khandu's visit, the protest turned violent; an MLA's house was attacked and there were allegations of vehicles being burnt. On 4 October police and paramilitary forces are alleged to have used lathis in Uggeng, on which the police declined to comment. According to local journalist Christina Pangam, people are against not just the study but the whole dam. The government cites the consent of 110 families of Geku village, but opponents say this is not the majority view.

The Adi community body Adi Bane Kebang United has demanded that the forces be withdrawn and the project scrapped, and its president Thomas Borang lists the dangers of such a big dam in an earthquake zone. The government argues that the dam will stop floods and serve as an answer to China's proposed 60,000 megawatt Medog dam.

Repression has grown along with the protest. The CBI has filed a case against Bhanu Tatak, legal adviser of the Siang Indigenous Farmers' Forum, for receiving 17.6 lakh rupees in foreign donations without FCRA registration. At least three protesters were summoned under the public property law, news from protest sites was blocked, and a local news channel's social media pages were shut down under the IT rules.
nazar: Deciding the future of a valley without asking the people who live on the river, and then filing cases against those who ask questions: this model of development is an old wound in the Northeast. The argument of competing with China has its place, but no project can last without the consent of the owners of the land on which the dam is to be built.
sawal: Where is the village's consent in a national race?
ref: Adi community
A large Adivasi (indigenous) community of Arunachal Pradesh, settled in the Siang valley and deeply tied to the river.
FCRA
The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, under which government registration is needed to receive foreign donations.
photo_note: Representative image: a hanging bridge in the Northeast

h: Death in detention: the truth of America's immigrant jails
dek: On Democracy Now!, Al Jazeera journalist Natasha Del Toro explains why people at the Adelanto detention centre in California are dying for lack of medical care.
by: Natasha Del Toro, in conversation with Amy Goodman and Juan Gonzalez
body: This is a segment of Democracy Now! in which Amy Goodman and Juan Gonzalez speak with Natasha Del Toro, an investigative correspondent for Al Jazeera English's programme Fault Lines. The conversation centres on Fault Lines' twenty-five-minute film 'Dying in Detention', released on 15 October, which investigates rising deaths in America's immigrant detention centres.

According to Democracy Now!, since the start of President Trump's second term at least 59 people have died in the custody of the immigration agency ICE, the highest number in more than a decade. According to a 2026 report by California's Attorney General, four of the five recent deaths at the Adelanto centre are linked to negligent medical care. The centre is run by the private prison company GEO Group.

Del Toro says the real count may be higher, because ICE's rules have been changed and it is no longer required to report some deaths linked to detention. The programme also mentions a 56-year-old permanent resident who died this month at a centre in Laredo, Texas, and who had been complaining to his daughter for months that he was not getting treatment.

At the heart of the film is the story of 39-year-old Ismael Ayala Uribe. He was brought to America from Mexico at the age of four or five, worked at a car wash for fifteen years and was caught in a raid. At Adelanto, despite a fever and a painful wound, he was at first given only painkillers. The infection turned into sepsis and he died after reaching hospital. His family learned of it not from ICE but from local police the next morning. According to the film, a doctor who reviewed his medical papers called the death preventable.

The conversation also turns to conditions inside the centre. Detainees have filed a lawsuit and gone on hunger strike. One detainee alleges that those who complain are put in solitary confinement as punishment, and another has alleged beatings.

The last part is about the link between money and power. According to Juan Gonzalez, the Department of Homeland Security has bought two Adelanto centres from GEO Group for 95 crore (950 million) dollars, but the same company will run them. Del Toro says the current ICE director was earlier a senior GEO official, and that the company has made huge profits from immigrant detention and given political donations. She fears that government ownership may make it harder to sue over conditions.
nazar: This conversation shows that when taking away a person's freedom becomes a profitable business for a company, their health and life slip to the bottom line of the accounts. A person in detention, from whatever country, has a right to medical care and dignity, and this is the responsibility of the state, not of a contractor.

Similar questions have been raised here too about the detention centres built for people declared foreigners. So this is not just America's story, but a mirror to every system that keeps human beings behind bars on the basis of paper.
sawal: Should detention centres be handed over to private companies?
ref: ICE
America's Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, which arrests, detains and deports immigrants without valid papers.
DACA
A programme that gives temporary protection from deportation and permission to work to undocumented people brought to America as children.

h: From a rented room to a letter addressed to the country
dek: Nine poems by young poet Vidhan Gunjan in Sammukh, which hold homelessness, the call of the village, patriarchy and the loneliness of old age side by side.
body: On 23 October Sammukh published nine poems by Vidhan Gunjan, calling him a committed and hopeful voice of young Hindi poetry today. We are not reproducing the poems here, only telling you what they revolve around.

The first two poems are about life in rented homes. One is about a man who has lived in rented houses for decades and has no permanent address left, as if he were a migrant in his own city. The second is about the day of leaving a house, when marks on the walls, kitchen smoke and slippers left behind show that some things cannot be packed with the luggage.

Then the poet's range widens. A letter addressed to the country carries the love of a citizen who gets nothing in return, and who sees that institutions stand with the powerful, not the honest. In a poem about soil, the village calls back those who left it for the city.

Two poems take on the male gaze directly. One is about men who pose as guardians of a woman's honour but really want to possess her. In the other, the image of a woman keeps changing with every sip of liquor, and this change exposes the man's double standards.
The other poems are about relationships slowly falling apart, time lost in separation, and old age, when all one's childhood friends are gone and a father has outlived his son.
nazar: A rented room is today the address of crores of Indians, especially young people who come to cities for work. Gunjan's poetry lifts this homelessness from private grief to a question of citizenship, and that is its strength.
It is also a good sign that a young poet questions so directly the thinking that calls control over women by the name of honour.
sawal: Where is the country of someone who has no permanent address?
ref: Sammukh
An online Hindi literary magazine that publishes poetry, stories, translations and criticism every day.
photo_note: A lane in Rania village, around 1816

h: A mismatched marriage, and grief that does not stay
dek: Pratyush Chandra Mishra's story looks with a slow, steady eye at the tangled years of a Patna government employee's marriage.
body: This story, published in Sammukh on 21 October, is about Sonu Babu, who lives in Patna. Polio has weakened his right leg, migraines trouble him, and he reads and writes poetry. After teaching at a school near Gaya, he passed a competitive exam and joined the statistics department at the block level.

Through an acquaintance from Chhapra, his marriage to Soni is arranged. After the wedding Soni keeps her distance and speaks little. Her insistence on cleanliness and order goes too far, and she avoids cooking or eating together. His mother and sister sense the tension, quarrels grow, and one night in anger Sonu Babu raises his hand on her.

The story does not justify this violence. Instead it paints a tired household in which even his younger brother's college form is not submitted because of an employee's carelessness. Sonu Babu consults a psychiatrist. A son is born, yet the knots in the home do not loosen.

When he is transferred, he moves to Gaya and comes to Patna on weekends. Two years later his life has settled a little: a story of his has been published, he has built a bond with his son, and books and films have come back. Soni too is more sensitive than before, but the relationship is more a matter of carrying on than of warmth.
The story ends not on a big decision but on the feeling that even grief does not stay for long.
nazar: In Hindi fiction, marriage is often either romantic or tragic. Mishra stays on the middle ground where most Indian marriages run, on compromise, silence and habit.

There may be a question of mental health behind Soni's behaviour, and the story avoids making her a villain. Still, the ease with which the narrative moves past the man raising his hand may trouble the reader.
sawal: Is a relationship that is simply carried on also a kind of love?
ref: Prakhand
The administrative unit below the district, also called a block. In Bihar much of the work on development and statistics is run from here.
photo_note: Shakuntala lost in thought, Ravi Varma

h: Viren-iyat 8: poetry of resistance in memory of Viren Dangwal
dek: Eight Hindi and Urdu poets were invited to the eighth edition of Viren-iyat, the Jan Sanskriti Manch's annual event, and Sammukh published a detailed notice about it.
body: On 9 October Sammukh published the Jan Sanskriti Manch's notice giving details of the eighth edition of Viren-iyat. The poetry reading was held that same evening at Jawahar Bhawan in New Delhi. Viren-iyat is held in memory of Hindi poet Viren Dangwal, who died on 28 September 2015.

According to the organisers, the series began in 2016, four editions were held till 2019, and after a pause it began again in 2023. What sets it apart is that there are no long speeches about Dangwal's life. The aim is to listen for where the concerns of his poetry show up in today's new poetry.
The notice describes Dangwal's poetry as deeply tied to the social and political realities of his time, written in simple language, with humour, warmth and faith in human beings.

This time eight poets were invited. Ibbar Rabbi as a poet of the lives and struggles of ordinary people, Anamika as a poet who gives women's experience a language of their own, Savita Singh as a poet of women's desire, love and loneliness, and Parvati Tirkey as a poet who catches the rhythm of Adivasi (indigenous) life.

Along with them were R. Chetan Kranti, Saumya Malviya, Usama, who is shaping a new language in Urdu, and Arbaz Khan, who gives voice to experiences targeted by the bulldozers of power. The organisers invited readers of both Hindi and Urdu.
nazar: The best way to remember a poet is not to build a statue but to carry forward their concerns. Viren-iyat does just that, and by bringing Hindi and Urdu poets onto one stage it also protects the shared culture that people are trying hard to divide today.
An Adivasi poet and a young man who writes on bulldozer politics sharing the stage shows where the poetry of resistance is coming from now.
sawal: Can a poetry reading still be a place of resistance today?
ref: Viren Dangwal
A beloved Hindi people's poet who won the Sahitya Akademi Award for 'Dushchakra Mein Srashta' (The Creator in a Vicious Circle). He taught in Bareilly.
Jan Sanskriti Manch
A Left-leaning organisation of writers and cultural workers that holds literary and cultural events.

h: Three poems by Anne Carson, translated by Jyoti Shobha
dek: On the occasion of the Nobel, Sammukh presented three poems by Anne Carson in Hindi, in which household detail, myth and the drama of grief move together.
body: After Anne Carson won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature, Sammukh published Hindi translations of three of her poems on 9 October. The translation is by poet Jyoti Shobha, whose collection 'Rupali Datta aur Anya Kavitayen' (Rupali Datta and Other Poems) has been widely discussed. We are not reproducing the poems here, only describing their mood.

The first poem is about the part of a family that is set aside as useless and sacrificed. In it there is a wedding no one came to, a cake eaten alone in the pantry, a lamplit room where grief is chewed slowly all night, and a telegram at one dollar for five words. There is deep sadness in short, broken lines.

The second poem comes from the world of Geryon in 'Autobiography of Red'. The teenage Geryon meets Herakles, and this meeting is recorded in ordinary images like two eels at the bottom of a tank, a bus station at three in the morning and railway tracks. The old myth comes down into today's ordinary surroundings.

The third poem thinks about grief in the form of questions and answers. Does watching others' suffering on stage wash away the darkness inside us? Carson's answer is that the actor goes down into that darkness in our place and, by giving a moment of his own life, gives us back our own story.
All three poems show that in Carson's work, Greek tragedy and the everyday home live in the same room.
nazar: After the Nobel, many articles on Carson appeared in Hindi, but the direct taste of her poetry can only come through translation. A Hindi poet doing the translation is also a guarantee that the poems have not merely passed through a dictionary.
Thinking about grief through Greek tragedy may also remind the Hindi reader of the idea of rasa in the Natyashastra, where the audience finds something within itself through the sorrow on stage.
sawal: Does someone else's acted-out sorrow lighten our own burden?
ref: Geryon
A red monster from Greek myth who is killed by Herakles. Carson turned him into a sensitive teenager.

h: Moriana: a city whose two faces never meet
dek: The twelfth part of Suman Shekhar's serial translation brings Moriana from Italo Calvino's 'Invisible Cities' and a conversation between Marco Polo and Kublai Khan.
body: Young fiction writer Suman Shekhar is translating Italo Calvino's famous book 'Invisible Cities' into Hindi in instalments on Sammukh. The twelfth part, out on 6 October, has three sections: an opening piece linked to the memory of a small town seen by Nirmal Verma, a conversation between Kublai Khan and Marco Polo about a garden, and Moriana from the 'Cities and Eyes' series.

Moriana appears from the mountain pass just as you cross the river, and at first sight it dazzles. Its gates look like transparent marble, its columns are of coral, its arches are set with green stones, and its glass mansions look like big aquariums in which shining dancers seem to swim.

But the traveller who has been there before knows that just half a turn around, the city's other face appears: rusted tin, sacks, planks with nails, soot-filled pipes, heaps of empty cans, walls with peeling posters.

Calvino's point is that Moriana has no depth. It is like a sheet of paper printed on both sides, whose two faces can neither be separated nor see each other. That is, the city's beauty and its misery are two sides of the same thing, and any onlooker can see only one side at a time. The one who enjoys the glitter stays unaware of the junk, and the one who lives in the junk stays unaware of the glitter.
Throughout the book, Marco Polo tells the old emperor stories of such cities, and each city is really a metaphor for one idea.
nazar: Reading about Moriana, one is bound to think of any Indian metro, where right behind the shining malls and flyovers lie slums, junk and stinking drains. 'Smart city' advertisements often show only the first face.
Such patient serial translations of world literature are rare in Hindi. That is why Suman Shekhar's work is valuable.
sawal: Which face of our city do we not want to see?
ref: Italo Calvino
A twentieth century Italian writer whose 'Invisible Cities' was published in 1972. In it Marco Polo tells Kublai Khan stories of imagined cities.
photo_note: Jahangir and Prince Khurram, Mughal painting

h: The depression hidden behind a smile: a young writer's first story
dek: Twenty-year-old Aryan Prajapati's story 'Havan' uses the image of a double to capture the depression growing inside a student living alone in the city.
body: On 5 October Sammukh published 'Havan' (a ritual fire offering), Aryan Prajapati's first published story. According to the magazine's introduction, he was born in 2006 in a village in Uttar Pradesh's Ambedkar Nagar district and completed Hindi Honours at Delhi's Hindu College this year.

The narrator, Mohan, lives alone in a rented room on the fourth floor of a five-storey building in a city. From outside all is well: he goes to class and sits with friends. His close friend Niranjan senses that Mohan is somewhere far away, but Mohan brushes it off with laughter and reassurance, and slowly learns to hide his pain so neatly that everyone thinks he is happy.

At midnight and in the afternoons, someone exactly like Mohan comes and sits with him, saying nothing, only watching. He grows stronger with Mohan's tears. In the story this double is a metaphor for the illness that eats away from within. Drugs and wandering at night only deepen the emptiness.

A call comes from his father at home asking whether he will come for Diwali, and the memory of the village fields breaks Mohan further. The story moves towards a tragic end that leaves the reader restless.
This story does not glorify depression. Instead it shows how deceptive looking fine from the outside can be.
nazar: Lakhs of young people who come to cities from villages and towns for coaching and college live alone in rooms like this, and talk of their mental health is still wrapped in shame. A twenty-year-old writer putting this on record is important testimony.

The story's lesson lies in Niranjan's character: accepting a friend's 'I'm fine' is not enough. If you or someone close to you is going through such a time, asking for help is not weakness. You can talk to the Tele-MANAS helpline at 14416.
sawal: Can we see past our friends' laughter?
ref: Doppelganger
In literature, a double or likeness of a character, often a symbol of their inner fear or illness.
Tele-MANAS
The Government of India's free mental health helpline, number 14416, which runs round the clock in many languages.
